title: Why isn't the sky violet? Your eyes explain it
alt_titles: Violet scatters more than blue. So why is the sky blue?
The sky should look violet. Here's why it doesn't
description:
Violet light scatters even more than blue, but less violet sunlight, some absorption high up and our eyes' weak violet sensitivity make the sky look blue.
Source: Rayleigh 1871 (scattering); Baez, UC Riverside Physics FAQ
#shorts #science #physics

title: Why you can't tickle yourself (the robot test)
alt_titles: A tickle robot showed why self-tickling fails
Your brain cancels your own touch. Here's the test
description:
Your brain predicts your own touch and turns it down. Add a 0.2-second delay with a tickle robot and self-touch feels like someone else's.
Source: Blakemore, Wolpert & Frith 1998; Blakemore, Frith & Wolpert 1999

title: Your GPS only works because Einstein was right
alt_titles: GPS clocks gain 38 microseconds a day. Here's why
Why GPS satellites run their clocks slow on purpose
description:
Speed slows GPS satellite clocks by ~7 microseconds a day; weaker gravity speeds them up by ~45. Engineers pre-tune them to cancel the net 38.
Source: Ashby 2003 (Living Reviews in Relativity); Pogge, Ohio State
#shorts #physics #relativity

title: The metal box that shrank the world
alt_titles: How one metal box slashed port loading costs
The 1956 trip that changed world trade
description:
In 1956 Malcom McLean's Ideal-X carried 58 containers. The real breakthrough was one shared standard, which cut loading costs (by McLean's figures) from $5.83 to ~16 cents a ton.
Source: Levinson, The Box (2006); Bernhofen, El-Sahli & Kneller 2016
#shorts #history #economics

title: The option nobody picks (and why it's there)
alt_titles: Why pricing pages include a useless option
The decoy effect: a choice built to be ignored
description:
A 'decoy' option nobody picks can push people toward the one next to it. But replications show it works mainly on neat tables of numbers, like pricing pages.
Source: Huber, Payne & Puto 1982; Frederick, Lee & Baskin 2014
#shorts #psychology #marketing

title: Why repeated lies start to feel true
alt_titles: Hear it enough and it feels true. Even if you know
The illusory truth effect, in under a minute
description:
Repetition makes claims feel truer, even ones you know are false, because familiar feels easy and easy feels true. Only completely absurd claims resist.
Source: Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino 1977; Fazio et al. 2015
#shorts #psychology #misinformation

title: A random number just changed your answer
alt_titles: A spinning wheel skewed people's guesses
Anchoring: the bias that passed the replication test
description:
In 1974 a wheel-of-fortune number shifted people's estimates by 20 points. Anchoring is one of the classic biases that replicated strongly in 2014.
Source: Tversky & Kahneman 1974; Klein et al. 2014 (Many Labs)
#shorts #psychology #cognitivebias

title: Would a crowd help you? Real CCTV says probably
alt_titles: The bystander effect vs 219 real CCTV clips
Crowds don't just watch. 2019 footage shows it
description:
A 1968 lab study found people help less when others are listening. But a study of 219 real CCTV-recorded conflicts found someone stepped in about 9 times in 10.
Source: Darley & Latané 1968; Philpot et al. 2019 (American Psychologist)
#shorts #psychology #bystandereffect

title: Does time really speed up as you age?
alt_titles: Time flies at every age. The real cause may be busyness
Why the years feel faster (it may not be age)
description:
In a survey of 1,865 adults, nearly everyone said time flies and age barely mattered, except for the last 10 years. Feeling busy predicted it better than routine did.
Source: Friedman & Janssen 2010 (Acta Psychologica); Wittmann & Lehnhoff 2005

title: Why your phone feels like a slot machine
alt_titles: Pigeons explain why you keep checking your phone
Unpredictable rewards: from pigeons to your feed
description:
Unpredictable rewards kept Skinner's pigeons pecking; feeds and likes work in a similar way. Whether it's true 'addiction' is still debated.
Source: Ferster & Skinner 1957; Lindström et al. 2021 (Nature Communications)
